Five books with Canadian ties are on the New York Times' 100 Notable Books of 2026 list.
Selected by the staff of the New York Times Book Review, the list features the "standout" fiction and nonfiction of the year.
Good People
Patmeena Sabit was born in Kabul and is now based in Toronto.

Her novel, Good People, follows the Sharaf family, who have finally achieved the American dream. They arrived as refugees and worked hard to live in a fancy neighbourhood and send their kids to the best schools. But when a horrific tragedy befalls the family, people begin to wonder what is actually happening behind closed doors.
Good People was on the 2026 Giller Prize shortlist and won the 2026 Westport Prize for Literature.
Weavingshaw
Heba Al-Wasity, born an Iraqi refugee in Libya, grew up in Canada and currently lives in the U.K., where she also works as a doctor.

Her novel, Weavingshaw, is a gothic fantasy romance about a woman with a secret: she can see the dead. When her brother falls sick, she knows she must find the Saint of Silence, who trades secrets for money, in order to afford a cure. But to strike a deal with the saint, she must find the ghost he's been looking for.
Korean Messiah
Jonathan Cheng, originally from Toronto, is the China bureau chief of The Wall Street Journal. His nonfiction book, Korean Messiah, was a finalist for the 2026 Cundill History Prize.
In Korean Messiah, Cheng, the former Korea bureau chief for The Wall Street Journal, looks at North Korea’s Kim dynasty and its ties to American Christianity.
Trash!
Simon Paré-Poupart is the Montreal-based author of Trash!, which was translated from French by Pablo Strauss.

Trash! is both a memoir and exposé drawing on Paré-Poupart's 20 years of experience as a garbage man. He started the job to pay for university, pursuing graduate studies in sociology and business, and worked as a journalist and social worker before coming back to waste management. In the book, he shares stories from his work and the hard labour it takes to take care of trash.

Muskism
Quinn Slobodian is a Canadian historian based in Boston.

He co-wrote Muskism, a nonfiction book that examines Elon Musk and his effect on society, with U.S.-based co-author Ben Tarnoff. The book explores "Muskism," an ideology rooted in Musk's worldview in which technocrats reign supreme and machines drive production.

Other notable books on the New York Times' list include American Hagwon by Min Jin Lee, Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke, Cool Machine by Colson Whitehead, The Disappearers by Marlon James, Taipei Story by R.F. Kuang and Whistler by Ann Patchett.
